name: Stalemate
summary: Stalemate is a draw when the side to move has no legal move and is not in check — here 1.Qf7 would throw away a winning queen.
intro: Stalemate is one of the rules that most often surprises the beginner: when the player to move has no legal move and yet is not in check, the game is not lost but immediately drawn. It is the great defensive resource of the endgame, letting a side that is hopelessly behind sometimes rescue half a point. For the side that is winning, it is a lurking hazard, because an over-eager queen or a far-advanced pawn can suddenly strip the lone king of every square. The diagram shows the most famous stalemate trap of all: White is a whole queen ahead with mate available, yet one careless move throws the win away.
boardCaption: White to move is a queen up, but 1.Qf7?? would stalemate the black king — a draw. The win is 1.Qg7 mate.

sections.heading: What stalemate is
paragraphs: Stalemate occurs when the side to move has no legal move available and its king is not in check. Unlike checkmate, it does not end the game in a win; it ends it immediately in a draw. The distinction is worth stressing, because the material on the board is irrelevant — a player a queen or more ahead scores only half a point if the opponent is stalemated.

For the defender this is the endgame's great saving grace. A side facing certain loss can sometimes steer deliberately into a stalemate and escape with a draw. For the stronger side the same possibility is a constant danger, especially when a queen or an advanced pawn takes away the enemy king's last squares.

sections.heading: The demonstration
paragraphs: In the diagram White is a whole queen up and has checkmate in one with 1.Qg7. The careless 1.Qf7, however, is a catastrophe. The black king on h8 is not in check, but it has no legal move: g7, g8, and h7 are all covered by the white queen and king.

With no move and no check, Black is stalemated, and the game is an immediate draw despite White's enormous material advantage. The winning move was the nearby 1.Qg7 mate. The two squares could hardly be closer, yet one is a full point and the other only a half.

sections.heading: Avoiding the trap
paragraphs: The practical rule when delivering mate is simple: always leave the enemy king at least one legal square until the very move that is checkmate. Checking blindly or grabbing squares with the queen too soon is how won games slip into stalemate draws.

It helps to distinguish stalemate from zugzwang, with which it is easily confused. In zugzwang a player has legal moves but every one of them is bad; in stalemate there are no legal moves at all. The first loses because you must move; the second draws because you cannot.

keyIdeas: Stalemate is when the side to move has no legal move and its king is not in check.
The result is an immediate draw, not a win for either side, whatever the material.
It is the endgame's great defensive resource: a losing side can sometimes force it to save a draw.
For the stronger side it is a constant hazard, especially with a queen or an advanced pawn.
When mating, always leave the enemy king a square until the move that is actually checkmate.
Stalemate differs from zugzwang: here you have no legal move at all, not merely a bad one.

white: Use the overwhelming material to force mate, keeping the enemy king a legal square until the mating move.
Deliver checkmate with 1.Qg7 rather than stalemating the king with 1.Qf7.
Never take away the last square of the lone king unless the move also gives check and mate.
black: Head for the corner and hope the stronger side blunders into stalemate.
Look for any position where a single careless move would leave you with no legal reply.
Remember that stalemate saves a draw no matter how far behind in material you are.
